section.heading: 8.3. Applications to Physics and Engineering
section.paragraph: Among the many applications of integral calculus to physics and engineering, we consider two here: force due to water pressure and centers of mass. As with our previous applications to geometry (areas, volumes, and lengths) and to work, our strategy is to break up the physical quantity into a large number of small parts, approximate each small part, add the results (giving a Riemann sum), take the limit, and then evaluate the resulting integral.
section.heading: Hydrostatic Pressure and Force
section.paragraph: Deep-sea divers know first-hand that water pressure increases as they dive deeper. This is because the weight of the water above them increases.

In general, suppose that a thin horizontal plate with area $$A$$ square meters is submerged in a fluid of density $$\rho$$ kilograms per cubic meter at a depth $$d$$ meters below the surface of the fluid as in Figure 1. The fluid directly above the plate (think of a column of liquid) has volume $$V = Ad$$ , so its mass is $$m = \rho V = \rho Ad$$ . The force exerted by the fluid on the plate is therefore
$$F = mg = \rho gAd$$
where $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The pressure $$P$$ on the plate is defined to be the force per unit area:
$$P = \frac{F}{A} = \rho gd$$

image.alt: Details A horizontal and approximately square shaped area, labeled A, immersed in a fluid at a depth d from its surface.

section.paragraph: The SI unit for measuring pressure is a newton per square meter, which is called a pascal (abbreviation: $$1N/m^{2} = 1{Pa}$$ ). Since this is a small unit, the kilopascal (kPa) is often used. For instance, because the density of water is $$\rho = 1000{kg}/m^{3}$$ , the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool $$2$$ m deep is
$$\begin{array}{l} {{P = \rho gd} = {1000{kg}/m^{3} \times 9.8m/s^{2} \times 2m}} \\ {\phantom{P = \rho gd} = {19,600{Pa} = 19.6{kPa}}} \end{array}$$

The pressure exerted on a submerged object by a fluid changes with depth but is independent of the volume of fluid. A fish swimming $$2$$ ft below the surface experiences the same water pressure whether in a small aquarium or an enormous lake.

When using US Customary units, we write $$P = \rho gd = \delta d$$ , where $$\delta = \rho g$$ is the weight density (as opposed to $$\rho$$ , which is the mass density). For instance, the weight density of water is $$\delta = 62.5{lb}/{ft}^{3}$$ , so the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool $$8{ft}$$ deep is $$P = \delta d = 62.5{lb}/{ft}^{3} \times 8{ft} = 500{lb}/{ft}^{2}$$ .

An important principle of fluid pressure is the experimentally verified fact that at any point in a liquid the pressure is the same in all directions. (A diver feels the same pressure on nose and both ears.) Thus the pressure in any direction at a depth $$d$$ in a fluid with mass density $$\rho$$ is given by
$$P = \rho gd = \delta d$$

This helps us determine the hydrostatic force (the force exerted by a fluid at rest) against a vertical plate or wall or dam. This is not a straightforward problem because the pressure is not constant but increases as the depth increases.

section.heading: Moments and Centers of Mass
section.paragraph: Our main objective here is to find the point $$P$$ on which a thin plate of any given shape balances horizontally as in Figure 5. This point is called the center of mass (or center of gravity) of the plate.

image.alt: Details An irregular layer resembling the sole of a foot. A tall cone with a sharp apex lies below the layer and its apex meets the layer at a marked point P, located at the broader side.

section.paragraph: We first consider the simpler situation illustrated in Figure 6, where two masses $$m_{1}$$ and $$m_{2}$$ are attached to a rod of negligible mass on opposite sides of a fulcrum and at distances $$d_{1}$$ and $$d_{2}$$ from the fulcrum. The rod will balance if

image.alt: Details A horizontal line segment with its left and right endpoints labeled m_1 and m_2 is balanced on a slender cone, placed below the line segment, labeled fulcrum, with its apex touching the line segment, such that the distance between m_1 and m_2 from the fulcrum is d_1 and d_2, respectively.

section.paragraph: This is an experimental fact discovered by Archimedes and called the Law of the Lever. (Think of a lighter person balancing a heavier one on a seesaw by sitting farther away from the center.)

Now suppose that the rod lies along the $$x$$ -axis with $$m_{1}$$ at $$x_{1}$$ and $$m_{2}$$ at $$x_{2}$$ and the center of mass at $$\overline{x}$$ . If we compare Figures 6 and 7, we see that $$d_{1} = \overline{x} - x_{1}$$ and $$d_{2} = x_{2} - \overline{x}$$ and so Equation 2 gives

image.alt: Details A horizontal line segment with its left and right endpoints labeled m_1 and m_2 is balanced on a slender cone, below the line segment, labeled fulcrum with its apex touching the line segment, are graphed on the positive x axis. The point m_1 is at the mark x_1 on the x axis, m_2 is at x_2, to the right of x_1, and the fulcrum is at x bar. The distance between m_1 and the fulcrum is labeled x bar minus x_1. The distance between m_2 and the fulcrum is labeled x_2 minus x bar.

section.paragraph: The numbers $$m_{1}x_{1}$$ and $$m_{2}x_{2}$$ are called the moments of the masses $$m_{1}$$ and $$m_{2}$$ (with respect to the origin), and Equation 3 says that the center of mass $$\overline{x}$$ is obtained by adding the moments of the masses and dividing by the total mass $$m = m_{1} + m_{2}$$ .

In general, if we have a system of $$n$$ particles with masses $$m_{1},m_{2},\ldots,m_{n}$$ located at the points $$x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}$$ on the $$x$$ -axis, it can be shown similarly that the center of mass of the system is located at
$$\overline{x} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{m_{i}x_{i}}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}m_{i}} = \frac{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{m_{i}x_{i}}}{m}$$
where $$m = \Sigma m_{i}$$ is the total mass of the system, and the sum of the individual moments
$$M = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}m_{i}x_{i}$$

is called the moment of the system about the origin. Then Equation 4 could be rewritten as $$m\overline{x} = M$$ , which says that if the total mass were considered as being concentrated at the center of mass $$\overline{x}$$ , then its moment would be the same as the moment of the system.

Now we consider a system of $$n$$ particles with masses $$m_{1},m_{2},\ldots,m_{n}$$ located at the points $$\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right),\left( x_{2},y_{2} \right),\ldots,\left( x_{n},y_{n} \right)$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane as shown in Figure 8. By analogy with the one-dimensional case, we define the moment of the system about the $$y$$ -axis to be
$$M_{y} = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}m_{i}x_{i}$$
and the moment of the system about the $$\mathbf{x}$$ -axis as
$$M_{x} = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}m_{i}y_{i}$$

image.alt: Details Three circles, labeled m_1, m_2, and m_3, are drawn on the x y coordinate plane. The circle m_1 is in the first quadrant at distances x_1 and y_1 from the x and y axes, respectively. The circle m_2 is in the fourth quadrant at distances x_2 and y_2 from the x and y axes, respectively. The circle m_3 is in the second quadrant at distances x_3 and y_3 from the x and y axes, respectively.

section.paragraph: Then $$M_{y}$$ measures the tendency of the system to rotate about the $$y$$ -axis and $$M_{x}$$ measures the tendency to rotate about the $$x$$ -axis.
As in the one-dimensional case, the coordinates $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ of the center of mass are given in terms of the moments by the formulas
$${\overline{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m}}{\overline{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m}}$$

where $$m = \sum m_{i}$$ is the total mass. Because $$m\overline{x} = M_{y}$$ and $$m\overline{y} = M_{x}$$ , the center of mass $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ is the point where a single particle of mass $$m$$ would have the same moments as the system.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the moments and center of mass of the system of objects that have masses $$3$$ , $$4$$ , and $$8$$ at the points $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , $$\left( {2, - 1} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {3,2} \right)$$ , respectively.
Solution We use Equations 5 and 6 to compute the moments:
Since $$m = 3 + 4 + 8 = 15$$ , we use Equations 7 to obtain
$$\overline{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{29}{15} \overline{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{15}{15} = 1$$
Thus the center of mass is $$\left( {1\frac{14}{15},1} \right)$$ . (See Figure 9.)

section.paragraph: The centroid of a region $$\mathcal{R}$$ is determined solely by the shape of the region. If a plate of uniform density occupies $$\mathcal{R}$$ , then its center of mass coincides with the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ . If, however, the density is not uniform, then typically the center of mass is at a different location. We will examine this situation in Section 15.4.

Next we consider a flat plate (called a lamina) with uniform density $$\rho$$ that occupies a region $$\mathcal{R}$$ of the plane. We wish to locate the center of mass of the plate, which is called the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ . In doing so we use the following physical principles: the symmetry principle says that if $$\mathcal{R}$$ is symmetric about a line $$l$$ , then the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ lies on $$l$$ . (If $$\mathcal{R}$$ is reflected about $$l$$ , then $$\mathcal{R}$$ remains the same so its centroid remains fixed. But the only fixed points lie on $$l$$ .) Thus the centroid of a rectangle is its center. Moments should be defined so that if the entire mass of a region is concentrated at the center of mass, then its moments remain unchanged. Also, the moment of the union of two nonoverlapping regions should be the sum of the moments of the individual regions.

Suppose that the region $$\mathcal{R}$$ is of the type shown in Figure 10(a); that is, $$\mathcal{R}$$ lies between the lines $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ , above the $$x$$ -axis, and beneath the graph of $$f$$ , where $$f$$ is a continuous function. We divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta x$$ . We choose the sample point $$x_{i}^{*}$$ to be the midpoint $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ of the $$i$$ th subinterval, that is, $${\overline{x}}_{i} = \left( x_{i - 1} + x_{i} \right)/2$$ . This determines the approximation to $$\mathcal{R}$$ by rectangles shown in Figure 10(b). The centroid of the $$i$$ th approximating rectangle $$R_{i}$$ is its center $$C_{i}{\left( {{\overline{x}}_{i},\frac{1}{2}f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)} \right)}$$ . Its area is $$f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)\Delta x$$ , so its mass is density × area:
$$\rho f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)\Delta x$$

section.paragraph: The moment of $$R_{i}$$ about the $$y$$ -axis is the product of its mass and the distance from $$C_{i}$$ to the $$y$$ -axis, which is $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ . Thus
$$M_{y}(R_{i}) = \left\lbrack {\rho f\left( \overline{x_{i}} \right)\Delta x} \right\rbrack{\overline{x}}_{i} = \rho{\overline{x}}_{i}f(\overline{x}i)\Delta x$$

Adding these moments, we obtain the moment of the polygonal approximation to $$\mathcal{R}$$ , and then by taking the limit as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ we obtain the moment of $$\mathcal{R}$$ itself about the $$y$$ -axis:
$$M_{y} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\rho{\overline{x}}_{i}f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)}\Delta x = \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{xf(x)dx}}$$
In a similar fashion we compute the moment of $$R_{i}$$ about the $$x$$ -axis as the product of its mass and the distance from $$C_{i}$$ to the $$x$$ -axis (which is half the height of $$R_{i}$$ ):
$$M_{x}(R_{i}) = \lbrack\rho f({\overline{x}}_{i})\Delta x\rbrack\frac{1}{2}f({\overline{x}}_{i}) = \rho \cdot \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right) \right\rbrack^{2}\Delta x$$
Again we add these moments and take the limit to obtain the moment of $$\mathcal{R}$$ about the $$x$$ -axis:

$$M_{x} = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\rho \cdot \frac{1}{2}\lbrack f(\overline{x})}\rbrack^{2}\Delta x = \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2}dx}}$$

Just as for systems of particles, the center of mass $$\left( \overline{x},\overline{y} \right)$$ of the plate is defined so that $$m\overline{x} = M_{y}$$ and $$m\overline{y} = M_{x}$$ . But the mass of the plate is the product of its density and its area:
$$m = \rho A = \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$
and so

$$\begin{array}{lllll} \overline{x} & = & \frac{M_{y}}{m} & = & {\frac{\rho{\int_{a}^{b}{xf(x)dx}}}{\rho{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}} = \frac{\int_{a}^{b}{xf(x)dx}}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}} \\ \overline{y} & = & \frac{M_{x}}{m} & = & {\frac{\rho{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2}dx}}}{\rho{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}} = \frac{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}dx}}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}} \end{array}$$
Notice the cancellation of the $$\rho$$ ’s. When density is constant, the location of the center of mass is independent of the density.
In summary, the center of mass of the plate (or the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ ) with area $$A$$ is located at the point $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ , where
$$\overline{x} = \frac{1}{A}{\int_{a}^{b}{xf(x)dx}} \overline{y} = \frac{1}{A}{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}}dx$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the center of mass of a semicircular plate of radius $$r$$ with uniform density.

Solution In order to use (8) we place the semicircle as in Figure 11 so that $$f(x) = \sqrt{r^{2} - x^{2}}$$ and $$a = - r$$ , $$b = r$$ . Here there is no need to use the formula to calculate $$\overline{x}$$ because, by the symmetry principle, the center of mass must lie on the $$y$$ -axis, so $$\overline{x} = 0$$ . The area of the semicircle is $$A = \frac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}$$ , so

$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{A}{\int_{- r}^{r}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- r}^{r}{\left( \sqrt{r^{2} - x^{2}} \right)^{2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}{\int_{0}^{r}{(r^{2} - x^{2})dx}} ({since the integrand is even})} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}\left\lbrack {r^{2}x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{r}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}\frac{2r^{3}}{3} = \frac{4r}{3\pi}} \end{array}$$
The center of mass is located at the point $$\left( {0,4r/\left( {3\pi} \right)} \right)$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find the centroid of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves $$y = \cos x$$ , $$y = 0$$ , and $$x = 0$$ .
Solution The area of the region is
$$A = {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos xdx = \sin x\rbrack_{0}^{\pi/2} = 1}}$$
so Formulas 8 give

$$\begin{array}{lll} \overline{x} & = & {\frac{1}{A}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{xf(x)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}x\cos xdx}}} \\ & = & {x\sin x\rbrack_{0}^{\pi/2} - {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\sin xdx ({by integration by parts})}}} \\ & = & {\frac{\pi}{2} - 1} \\ \overline{y} & = & {\frac{1}{A}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{2}}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2}dx = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos^{2}xdx}}} \\ & = & {\frac{1}{4}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{(1 + \cos 2x)dx = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack {x + \frac{1}{2}\sin 2x} \right\rbrack}}_{0}^{\pi/2} = \frac{\pi}{8}} \end{array}$$
The centroid is $$\left( {\frac{1}{2}\pi - 1,\frac{1}{8}\pi} \right) \approx (0.57,0.39)$$ and is shown in Figure 12.

section.paragraph: If the region $$\mathcal{R}$$ lies between two curves $$y = f(x)$$ and $$y = g(x)$$ , where $$f(x) \geqslant g(x)$$ , as illustrated in Figure 13, then the same sort of argument that led to Formulas 8 can be used to show that the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ is $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ , where

$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{x} = \frac{1}{A}{\int_{a}^{b}{x\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack dx}}} \\ {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{A}{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left\{ {\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2}\left. {- \left\lbrack g(x) \right\rbrack^{2}} \right\} dx} \right.}}} \end{array}$$
(See Exercise 51.)

example.paragraph: Find the centroid of the region bounded by the line $$y = x$$ and the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ .

section.heading: Theorem of Pappus
section.paragraph: We end this section by showing a surprising connection between centroids and volumes of revolution.

note.title: Theorem of Pappus
note.heading: Theorem of Pappus
note.paragraph: Let $$\mathcal{R}$$ be a plane region that lies entirely on one side of a line $$l$$ in the plane. If $$\mathcal{R}$$ is rotated about $$l$$ , then the volume of the resulting solid is the product of the area $$A$$ of $$\mathcal{R}$$ and the distance $$d$$ traveled by the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ .

section.paragraph: This theorem is named after the Greek mathematician Pappus of Alexandria, who lived in the fourth century ad.

section.heading: Discovery Project Complementary Coffee Cups
section.paragraph: Suppose you have a choice of two coffee cups of the type shown, one that bends outward and one inward, and you notice that they have the same height and their shapes fit together snugly. You wonder which cup holds more coffee. Of course you could fill one cup with water and pour it into the other one but, being a calculus student, you decide on a more mathematical approach. Ignoring the handles, you observe that both cups are surfaces of revolution, so you can think of the coffee as a volume of revolution.

From k, a vertical line rises upward. From h, a horizontal line segment extends rightward brushing past the starting point of the curve, until it reaches the line x = k, thus creating a rectangle.
